findings.heading: Slice rows per group / slice()
findings.proposition: The French says slice_min() selects the n rows with the SMALLEST values in the order_by column; the English says slice_min() selects the n rows with the HIGHEST values.
findings.reader_consequence: The two handbooks give opposite descriptions of the same function. The French matches actual dplyr behaviour, so an English reader who follows the English text picks the wrong end of the distribution, and a bilingual reader cannot tell which page to trust.

findings.heading: Slice rows per group / slice()
findings.proposition: The French says slice_max() selects the n rows with the LARGEST values in the order_by column; the English says slice_max() selects the n rows with the LOWEST values.
findings.reader_consequence: Same inversion in the other direction. The French statement is the correct dplyr behaviour, so the two language editions contradict each other on which rows slice_max() returns.

findings.heading: Linelist cases into days / Grouper par jours (linelist)
findings.proposition: The French says the first line of the chunk drops cases that have no 'date de rentrée' (date of entry/admission); the code drops rows missing date_onset, which the rest of the French chapter itself glosses as 'date de debut des symptomes' (date of symptom onset).
findings.reader_consequence: A French reader takes date_onset to mean an admission or entry date, and will reuse drop_na(date_onset) believing it filters on admission, mis-defining the denominator of every daily count that follows.

findings.heading: Select on grouped data / select() sur les donnees groupees
findings.proposition: The French instructs the reader to use ungroup() 'avant de degrouper' (before ungrouping); the English instructs the reader to use ungroup() before the select(), so that the grouping columns are not force-included.
findings.reader_consequence: The French sentence is circular and names no operation to place ungroup() before, so a reader does not learn that ungroup() must precede select() and keeps getting grouping columns they did not ask for.

findings.heading: Linelist cases into days / Grouper par jours (linelist)
findings.proposition: The English notes that the first rows of the resulting table skip over dates on which no cases occurred; the French does not state this.
findings.reader_consequence: The French reader loses the observation that motivates the whole section. Without seeing that empty days are absent from the output, the following complete() step reads as optional decoration rather than as the fix for a real gap in the time series.

findings.heading: Slice rows per group / slice()
findings.proposition: The English states that with_ties = TRUE keeps ties in slice_max(); the French entry for slice_max() omits the with_ties argument entirely (it keeps it for slice_min()).
findings.reader_consequence: A French reader assumes ties are handled differently by slice_max() than by slice_min(), or does not learn the argument exists there, and silently drops tied records when taking the top n per group.

findings.heading: Un-group / Degrouper les donnees
findings.proposition: The English warns that forgetting to ungroup can lead to incorrect calculations; the French warns only to remember to ungroup before steps that need the complete ungrouped dataset, and never states that the results can be wrong.
findings.reader_consequence: A French reader treats ungroup() as tidiness rather than as a correctness requirement, and has no reason to suspect a silently wrong denominator or total when they forget it.

findings.heading: Add counts / Ajouter des colonnes contenant les decomptes
findings.proposition: The French introduces add_tally() alongside add_count(); the English names only add_count().
findings.reader_consequence: A French reader is pointed at a function the chapter never demonstrates and whose grouping requirement differs from add_count(): add_tally() needs a prior group_by(), so calling it the way the chunk calls add_count(hospital) fails or returns a single overall count.

findings.heading: Slice rows per group / slice()
findings.proposition: The French states that replace = TRUE gives sampling with replacement in slice_sample(); the English says only that slice_sample() randomly selects n rows.
findings.reader_consequence: Content only French readers receive. It is correct, but the two editions no longer describe the same function surface, so a reviewer comparing them cannot tell whether the English is out of date or the French is unsourced.

findings.heading: Linelist cases into weeks / Grouper par semaines (linelist)
findings.proposition: The French states that floor_date(unit = "week") rounds each date to the first day of its week; the English makes this rounding claim only in the months section, not in the weeks section.
findings.reader_consequence: Content only French readers receive. It is correct, but it is propositional content the English weeks section does not carry, so the two editions explain floor_date() at different depths.
